claims.text: In sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, surface-energy minimization overrides sluggish diffusion.
Surface-energy gradients drive non-equilibrium segregation of Au and Cu to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu subsequently evaporate.
The proposed mechanism becomes dominant above a critical temperature at which surface-to-volume effects exceed entropic stabilization.
PLD-grown sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles initially possess a kinetically trapped FCC structure.
Nanoscale dimensions remove bulk-diffusion constraints in particles smaller than 10 nm.
Local lattice distortion is present at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-energy gradients and local lattice distortion lower the activation energy for Au and Cu surface diffusion relative to bulk diffusion.
At elevated temperature, the surface-free-energy term dominates configurational-entropy stabilization.
Au and Cu surface diffusion creates a core depleted in those elements.
Au/Cu surface enrichment lowers the local melting point.
Au/Cu surface enrichment increases vapor pressure and thereby causes selective Au/Cu evaporation.
Heating-driven surface-energy minimization reshapes elliptical or icosahedral particles into spheres with lower surface area.
A high surface diffusion coefficient and short diffusion paths negate bulk sluggish-diffusion behavior in sub-5 nm particles.
Differential evaporation causes progressive particle-mass loss and widening of the particle-size distribution.
After segregation, the FCC structure persists with an Au/Cu-rich shell and a Pt/Ni/Co-rich core.
High configurational entropy can stabilize a uniform single-phase multicomponent material.
For particles smaller than 10 nm, the surface-energy term is comparable to or greater than the bulk free-energy term.
For particles larger than 50 nm, sluggish diffusion dominates and segregation is minimal or absent.
The segregation-onset temperature depends on whether the initial particle shape is icosahedral or truncated octahedral.
